title: Data center power verification: the five rungs of evidence that a site can be powered
description: How to verify data center power at a site: the five rungs of power evidence, how to grade a broker's MW claim, and what to ask the utility to move a site up a rung.
intro: A data center site can be powered when a utility or grid operator has said so in writing for this load, at this location, by a date. Everything short of that is a lead. Most sites marketed as powered land rest on a map showing a substation nearby, which is the weakest evidence there is. This guide sorts power claims into five rungs, from a map to a metered connection, shows the documents that sit on each rung, and explains how a buyer can grade a broker's megawatt figure and push a site higher before spending money on parcels, surveys or options.
takeaways: Distance to a substation tells you almost nothing about spare capacity. In one 2025 ERCOT study, only about 17% of substations near suitable land had any withdrawal headroom.
Grade every power claim by the document behind it. A named MW figure is rung 2 until a current utility letter or study for this load is in hand.
Queue and pipeline totals overstate deliverable power by a wide margin. ERCOT's large-load queue passed 470 GW in 2026, far above what it has classified for study.
Kill disqualified sites before parcel work, then tier the rest: A documented power, B a named power path with a date, C land near capacity.

sections.heading: Proximity to a substation is the weakest evidence

blocks.text: The usual site pitch starts with a parcel and a line on a map: 200 acres, two miles from a 345 kV substation. That tells you where the wires are. It says nothing about whether the station or the lines behind it can carry another few hundred megawatts without overloading something under contingency. A buyer who searches by distance to a substation is screening for the cheapest attribute to check and the least predictive one.

Paces put numbers on this for Texas in a November 2025 white paper. Its team screened every Texas parcel against common developer criteria (at least 100 acres, slope under 15 degrees, favorable zoning, within 3 miles of a 345 kV substation or 1 mile of a 345 kV line, plus fiber and gas). It then added load bus by bus in ERCOT's 2028 summer-peak planning case, with full AC N-1 contingency analysis, until the first element overloaded. Only about 230 substations had suitable land within 3 miles, and only about 17% of the substations near those sites showed positive withdrawal capacity. The rest of the land was, in the paper's word, stranded.

The same paper found that five overloaded elements limited headroom for roughly 250,000 acres, about 30% of the viable land. So a single transmission constraint can disqualify dozens of parcels that look identical on a map. Land data vendors now say the same thing in their own marketing. LandGate, for one, argues that power availability has to be confirmed with current numbers before any other site factor is seriously evaluated, and that a cheap, well located parcel with no grid capacity nearby is not a viable site.

The practical conclusion is to search from power evidence first and only then look for land. Start with places where a utility, a planning record or an existing connection already shows megawatts. Parcels come second.

sections.heading: The five rungs of power evidence

blocks.text: We sort every power claim into one of five rungs, numbered 0 to 4. The rung is set by the strongest document in hand, not by what the seller says the document would show. A site can only be graded as high as its paperwork.

rows: 0: map only
Nothing about power. A parcel with no identified line or station of the right voltage.
Broker flyer, aerial, listing with "power nearby"
Nothing to check yet
1: proximity
A line or substation of a suitable voltage is near the parcel. No capacity figure.
Utility service territory map, transmission line map, distance study
Utility and ISO system maps, EIA-860 plant locations for nearby generation
2: named MW at a named station
Someone with authority has put a MW figure on a specific station, or an existing large connection is there to reuse.
Utility economic development site sheet, preliminary power plan, ISO planning case or load forecast entry, retired plant with known nameplate, an energized industrial load being vacated
EIA-860 and 860M retired and planned generators, ISO load forecasts and planning cases, utility site programs
3: study or approval for this load
The utility or grid operator has studied or approved this specific load at this site.
Load study or facilities study results, ERCOT large load classification, security posted, conditional will-serve letter tied to a load letter
ISO large load reports, PUC dockets for large load tariffs and contracts
4: signed or energized
Service is contracted with a date, or the load is already metered.
Executed electric service agreement or interconnection agreement with an in-service date, meter and billing history
PUC filings of special contracts, utility earnings disclosures of executed agreements

blocks.text: Two points about the middle rungs. Rung 2 includes existing connections, and these are often the best leads in a market. A retired or retiring generator had an export path sized to its nameplate, and EIA-860 lists generators by status, including retired and proposed units. EIA notes that the annual file's retired list covers only the current cycle, so use the monthly 860M inventory for a complete retirement history back to 2002. A retired plant's export path does not convert to load service automatically, but it does tell you where the transmission was built.

Rung 3 is where most real projects stall. Dominion Energy's Virginia process is a clear example of the steps. A customer files a site plan, a load letter and a load ramp through Dominion's data center portal. Dominion's team can then prepare an infrastructure evaluation and preliminary power plan, and a will-serve letter if needed. Dominion says projects over 50 MW will likely need a transmission extension and a new substation, and it often phases service with a bridging solution while the final plan is built. A preliminary power plan for your load is rung 3. A generic statement that the area has capacity is rung 2 at best.

sections.heading: Queues and pipelines overstate available power

blocks.text: Headline demand numbers are useful for understanding how crowded a grid is. They are useless as evidence that any one site has power. Requests are cheap to file, and the same project often files at several utilities. The gap between requested load and studied or signed load is the clearest measure of how much of the market is speculative.

blocks.text: ERCOT's numbers show the pattern at scale. The grid operator told the Texas Senate in July 2026 that it was tracking about 474 GW of large loads seeking interconnection. For comparison, its own September 2026 board deck listed conditional Batch Zero classifications of 66.4 GW as base load and 127.9 GW as studied load, and it excluded 302.2 GW. Those classifications were themselves conditional on an eligibility audit, with ERCOT asking for evidence such as purchase orders for long-lead equipment, real estate agreements, land use approvals and end-user agreements.

Utility disclosures tell the same story from the other end. Oncor reported 298 GW of service requests in its second quarter 2026 results, while 44 GW of its large load projects qualified for Batch Zero. Duke Energy separates executed agreements (7.6 GW) from a broader 15.4 GW pipeline that includes prospective load. PJM said its January 2026 forecast reflected improved vetting of requested data center adjustments and that it would derate longer-term projects without firm commitments. When a seller cites a utility's pipeline as proof that power is coming to their area, they are quoting the soft number.

Texas also shows how policy can freeze a rung. In August 2026 Governor Abbott directed the PUC and ERCOT to audit data centers in the interconnection process. ERCOT paused energization of new large-load data centers and crypto mining facilities pending that audit and a community impact review, with both reports due to the PUC by December 10, 2026. A September directive extended the pause to TCEQ permits. As of November 2026 we have not seen a public notice lifting it, so any Texas claim of a near-term energization date needs to say how it clears the audit.

sections.heading: How to grade a broker's power claim

blocks.text: Take a common pitch: "450 MW available, utility confirmed." Grade it by asking for the document, then reading the document for five things. Until a current utility letter is in hand, the claim is rung 2 at most, and if the MW figure has no named station behind it, it is rung 1.

items: Who wrote it. A utility, a transmission owner or an ISO counts. A broker summary of a phone call does not.
Which station and voltage. A MW figure without a named substation or line is a guess about the area, not the site.
Which load. A study for a 100 MW load does not cover 450 MW, and a study for someone else's project does not transfer to you without the utility saying so.
What date. Capacity in 2031 after a new 345 kV line is different from capacity at energization. Ask for the enabling projects and their status.
How old it is. Letters and studies age out as other loads sign. Treat anything over about a year old as needing refresh.

blocks.text: Then ask whether the seller has filed or paid for anything. A load letter on file, a study fee paid or security posted moves a claim toward rung 3, because it means the utility has a record of this load. In ERCOT, loads in the Batch Zero process had to bring financial security to $50,000 per MW. A seller who cannot show any of this is selling land and a hope.

Watch for borrowed evidence. A will-serve letter issued to a previous owner for a different load, a slide from a utility investor presentation, or a county's statement that a new substation is planned are all real documents. None of them is a study of your load.

sections.heading: How to move a site up a rung

blocks.text: Going from rung 1 to rung 2 takes a phone call. Going from rung 2 to rung 3 takes a filing, a fee and usually months. Before you spend money on the second step, make sure the first step held up.

Start with the utility's economic development or large load team, not the local customer service line. Investor-owned utilities and many cooperatives have staff whose job is to answer site questions for large loads. Ask them for a short list of facts in writing:

items: The serving substation and voltage they would expect to use for a load of your size at this parcel.
Whether that station or the lines feeding it have capacity today, and if not, what upgrades would be needed and roughly when.
Whether other large loads are already studying or signed at the same station. You are not asking for names, only whether you would be behind someone.
The formal intake steps for a load of your size: load letter, study request, study fee, security and expected study time.
Whether a preliminary power plan or conditional will-serve letter is available before a full study.

blocks.text: Going to rung 3 means filing. In Dominion's territory that is the load letter, site plan and ramp through its portal. In Texas, the PUC adopted large load interconnection standards in September 2026 that set a flat $100,000 study fee regardless of load size and dropped a proposed $50,000 per MW non-refundable fee. The final rule also gives 24 months of notice on missed energization milestones, applied to the schedule as a whole. Other utilities set their own fees and security through tariffs filed at their state commission, so read the current large load tariff in the PUC docket before budgeting.

Going to rung 4 means signing. An electric service agreement or interconnection agreement with an in-service date, minimum demand terms and security is the strongest evidence short of a meter. Read the conditions. A signed agreement that depends on a transmission project that has not cleared its own approvals carries that project's schedule risk.

sections.heading: Kill disqualifiers first, then assign a tier

blocks.text: Power evidence decides where to look. A kill sheet decides which of those places to drop before anyone pays for title work or a survey. We check these at the station level, then at the parcel level:

items: Already claimed: the capacity is under study, signed or operating for another load.
Already controlled: the land is under option, under contract or listed with terms that rule out the buyer.
Owner is an environmental-liability buyer that bought a retired plant to hold the remediation, not to sell the land.
Coal ash, landfill or contamination on or next to the developable area.
A county moratorium, pending zoning change or recent denial for data centers.

blocks.text: What survives gets a tier. Tier A is documented power: rung 3 or 4 evidence for this load at this site. Tier B is a named power path with a date: rung 2 evidence, a named station, the upgrades identified and a utility estimate of when they finish. Tier C is land near capacity: rung 1, a good parcel near the right voltage with no figure from anyone who would have to deliver it. Each tier comes with the next document that would move the site up, so a buyer knows what to ask for and who should produce it.

This is how Invariant screens sites before any introduction. We work from power records outward, run the kill sheet, and send a buyer the tier and the supporting documents together. If you have a requirement in MW, a state and an energize-by date, we can tell you what evidence exists in that market and what it would take to get a site from C to A.

faqs.question: How do I check if a data center site has power available?
faqs.answer: Ask for the document behind the claim and grade it. A utility study, approval or signed service agreement for your specific load is real evidence. A map showing a nearby substation is not, because nearby stations often have no spare headroom. Paces found only about 17% of substations near suitable Texas land had positive withdrawal capacity.

faqs.question: Is a will-serve letter proof of power for a data center?
faqs.answer: It depends on what it says and who it was issued for. Dominion describes a will-serve letter as one output of its site evaluation, alongside a preliminary power plan, ahead of design, rights of way and construction. Read it for the load size, station, date and conditions, and confirm it was issued for your project.

faqs.question: Why are large load interconnection queues so much bigger than what gets built?
faqs.answer: Filing a request is cheap, so developers file early and often at several utilities. ERCOT reported about 474 GW of large loads seeking interconnection in mid-2026, while its September 2026 conditional Batch Zero classifications covered about 194 GW and excluded 302.2 GW. Signed agreements are a much smaller number again.

faqs.question: What does it cost to get a large load study in Texas?
faqs.answer: Under the large load interconnection standards the Texas PUC adopted in September 2026, the study fee is a flat $100,000 regardless of load size. Loads in ERCOT's Batch Zero process also had to post financial security of $50,000 per MW. Check the current PUC rule and your transmission provider's process before budgeting.

faqs.question: Can a retired power plant site be used for a data center?
faqs.answer: Often it is one of the better leads, because the transmission was built for the plant's output. EIA-860 and its monthly 860M inventory list retired and planned generators with their capacity. The export path still has to be studied for load service, and the site needs a check for coal ash, contamination and who owns the remediation.

title: Will-serve letter vs load study vs ESA: which utility documents prove a data center site has power
description: Will-serve letter, load study, facilities study or ESA: what each utility document proves about data center power, what it doesn't, and the red flags to check.
intro: A will-serve letter shows a utility is willing to serve. It doesn't show that power will be there. Capacity a buyer can rely on is set by a load study for the specific load, held by a signed construction agreement with security, and priced by an electric service agreement that fixes the ramp, minimum bill and term. Read every power document in a land deal by where it sits in that sequence, and treat a seller's will-serve as a lead to verify, not proof.
takeaways: A will-serve letter states intent under tariff and is conditional. It doesn't reserve MW or fix a date.
A load study for the marketed load, at a named point of service, is the first document worth underwriting.
Signed construction agreements and posted security are the first commitment that costs someone real money.
New large-load tariffs bring minimum bills near 80 to 85% of contract demand and terms of 12 to 15 years. Model them before price.

sections.heading: Utilities issue power documents in a fixed order

blocks.text: Every utility uses its own names, yet the sequence for a large load is close to universal. A customer asks. The utility answers informally. Then it studies the specific load, prices the work, asks for money, and signs a contract that sets the ramp and the bill. Energization comes last. Each step costs the customer more and binds the utility a little more.

items: Inquiry response or capacity indication: an email or call note saying the area might support a load.
Will-serve or ability-to-serve letter: a signed statement that the utility intends to serve, subject to conditions.
Load study or system impact study: an engineering review of this load, at this point of service, on this ramp.
Facilities study and cost estimate: the substation, line and upgrade scope, with a price and schedule.
Letter of agreement, construction agreement or engineering agreement, usually with security or a reimbursement obligation.
Electric service agreement (ESA) under the applicable tariff: contract capacity, ramp, minimum bill, term, exit terms.
Energization: equipment in service, meter set, and in ERCOT a written approval to energize.

blocks.text: Dominion Energy's public process in Virginia follows that shape. It offers an infrastructure evaluation and preliminary power plan for sites under consideration, plus a will-serve letter if required. A formal project then needs a site plan, a load letter and a load ramp schedule before Dominion develops short-term and long-term power plans and moves into design, right-of-way acquisition, permitting, procurement, regulatory filings and construction.
The skill in diligence is knowing which rung a document sits on. A seller's data room rarely labels it for you.

sections.heading: Capacity indications and will-serve letters commit to very little

blocks.text: An inquiry response tells you the utility engineer didn't laugh. That's useful for screening and worth nothing for valuation. It is usually unsigned, undated in any formal sense, and based on a desk look at the nearest substation without any study of the load.

The will-serve letter is a step up because someone signs it. Read what it actually says, though. Most letters state that the utility is willing to provide service under its tariff and rules, subject to studies, facilities, agreements and payment. That's close to restating the utility's legal obligation to serve customers in its territory. It is not a reservation of megawatts at a date. Dominion lists the will-serve letter alongside its preliminary evaluation work, ahead of the site plan, load letter and ramp that a formal project requires.

Check five things on any letter. Is the MW figure named, and does it match the buyer's ultimate load or only phase one? Is a substation or point of service named? Is there a date, and is it an energization date or just the date of the letter? Does it expire? Who signed it, an account manager or someone in transmission or distribution planning? A letter that names no MW, no station and no date is a courtesy. In practice many letters are issued for zoning, financing or permit applications and say so on their face.

Capacity also moves. A letter written eighteen months ago described a queue that has since filled. Paces looked at ERCOT substations with suitable land nearby and found only about 17% showed positive withdrawal capacity, meaning room to add load without worsening existing overloads. A nearby substation is not headroom.

sections.heading: Load studies are the first document a buyer can underwrite

blocks.text: A load study models this load at this location. It tells you whether the existing system can carry it, which upgrades are needed, and roughly when. Utilities now charge for it and gate it behind site control, which is exactly why a completed study means something.

AEP Ohio's process is a clear public example. Data center requests of 25 MW or more go through PowerClerk, and the customer must control the property and state the location, load ramp and final load. The study fee is $10,000 for loads above 25 MW and under 50 MW, $50,000 for 50 MW to under 100 MW, and $100,000 at 100 MW and above. Unpaid fees mean the request is treated as withdrawn. AEP targets completion in 45 days, or 60 days when regional transmission upgrades are needed. As of November 2026 AEP is running studies in tranches, and its second 2026 tranche closed to applications on September 30, 2026.

Texas raised the bar further. In September 2026 the Public Utility Commission of Texas adopted interconnection rules for large loads under Senate Bill 6, setting a flat $100,000 study fee for every large load customer and dropping a proposed non-refundable fee of $50,000 per MW. If a customer misses its energization schedule by 24 months, the utility applies the customer's financial security to amounts owed and returns the balance. Utility Dive reported the rules were adopted during a pause on new data center interconnections meant to allow an audit of ERCOT's roughly 474 GW queue, about 90% of it data centers.

The Berkeley Lab and Brattle review of 55 large-load tariffs found that explicit study requirements, usually paid by the customer, are moderately common and increasing in tariffs proposed since 2025. Examples include development deposits that the utility draws down and refunds if unused.

What a study does not do is hold capacity. It reflects the queue on the day it ran. Ask for the study date, the assumed ramp, the list of required upgrades, and whether the utility will honor the result if the contracts are signed within a set window. A study for 100 MW doesn't support a 300 MW campus plan.

sections.heading: Construction agreements and security are the first real commitment

blocks.text: The facilities study turns the load study into a scope and a price: the new substation or bay, the line extension, transmission upgrades, and who pays for each. The utility will not order a transformer on a promise. Before it spends, it wants a signed agreement with money behind it.

AEP Ohio presents two contracts after the study. The Letter of Agreement makes the customer reimburse 100% of buildout costs if it cancels or delays the project more than 12 months before the target energization date, an obligation that ends when the project is complete. The ESA carries a good-faith energization estimate. Both must be signed within 60 days or the customer loses its place.

Collateral is where tariffs now bite. AEP Ohio requires a guarantee or collateral equal to 50% of total minimum charges over the full term, due at signing, with an exemption only for customers rated at least A- by S&P and A3 by Moody's with large cash balances. Surety bonds aren't accepted. Dominion's GS-5 schedule requires collateral of $1.5 million per MW of contracted capacity.

For a land buyer this rung matters most. Signed construction agreements and posted security mean someone with a balance sheet decided the site was worth real dollars. Ask who posted it, though. If the security belongs to a prior developer, it may not move with the land.

sections.heading: The ESA sets the ramp, the minimum bill and the way out

blocks.text: The electric service agreement is the contract that governs the bill for a decade or more. Under the new large-load tariffs it fixes contract capacity, the ramp schedule, the minimum billing demand, the term, collateral and the exit fee. A buyer reading an ESA should model the minimum bill as a fixed cost, because that's what it is.

blocks.text: Read the ramp closely. AEP's tariff sets minimum contract capacity at 50% in year one, rising to 90% in year four, and the contract term starts at actual energization. Dominion's GS-5 requires the load to ramp at least 20% of contracted capacity a year. Staged service also shows up in the utility's plan itself. Dominion describes serving load in stages as a bridge while the final power plan is built, so a 300 MW ESA may deliver a fraction of that on day one.

Georgia's rule lets Georgia Power bill customers above 100 MW for upstream generation, transmission and distribution costs as construction progresses, and requires every such contract to go to the PSC for review. For a Georgia site, ask whether the contract has been filed and where the review stands.

Utility Dive counted 264 large-load tariff filings in Halcyon's tracker by mid-August 2026. The terms above will keep moving. Check the tariff in force on the day you sign, not the one quoted in last year's deck.

sections.heading: How to read a seller's will-serve letter in a land deal

blocks.text: A listing that says "450 MW available, will-serve in hand" is making a claim about power, not land. Map it to an evidence ladder. Rung 0 is a map with nothing behind it. Rung 1 is proximity to a line or substation of the right voltage. Rung 2 is a named MW figure at a named station from a utility or planning record, or an existing large connection such as a retired plant's export or an energized load. Rung 3 is a utility study or approval for this load: a load study, a facilities study, security posted. Rung 4 is an executed service or interconnection agreement with a date, or service energized and metered.
Most seller will-serve letters land on rung 2 at best. They become rung 3 only when a study for the marketed load sits behind them.

items: Ask for the letter itself, not a summary. Read the conditions paragraph first.
Match the MW, the point of service and the customer name to the deal. A letter issued to a prior developer for 60 MW says little about a 400 MW campus.
Find the date and any expiry. Old letters describe old queues.
Ask whether a load study was requested, paid for and completed, and get a copy.
Ask whether the letter, study position or security is assignable to a buyer, and get the utility to confirm in writing.
Call the utility's large-load or economic development team with the seller's permission and confirm the request is still active.
Model the applicable large-load tariff's minimum bill, term and collateral before agreeing on price.

blocks.text: Then sort the site. Tier A has documented power, rung 3 or 4. Tier B has a named power path with a date, usually a current utility letter tied to a study in progress. Tier C is land near capacity and should be priced as land. Kill disqualifiers before any of this: the site already claimed or operating, under option, listed widely, owned by an environmental-liability buyer, carrying coal ash or contamination, or sitting in a county with a moratorium.

Energization is its own gate. In ERCOT, since October 2025, any load studied as a large load needs written approval from ERCOT's Large Load Integration team before the utility may energize it. A signed ESA doesn't replace that step.
Invariant screens sites this way before any introduction. The power documents get read and placed on the ladder first, and the parcel comes second.

faqs.question: Is a utility will-serve letter a guarantee of power for a data center?
faqs.answer: No. A will-serve letter usually states the utility's intent to serve under its tariff, subject to studies, facilities, agreements and payment. It does not reserve megawatts or fix an energization date. Capacity is set by a load study and held by signed agreements with security.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a load study and a facilities study?
faqs.answer: A load study tests whether the system can carry a specific load at a specific point and lists the upgrades needed. A facilities study turns that into a detailed scope, cost estimate and schedule for the utility work. Many utilities fold both into one study for distribution-level loads.

faqs.question: How much does a utility load study cost for a data center?
faqs.answer: It depends on the utility. AEP Ohio charges $10,000 to $100,000 depending on load size, starting above 25 MW. Texas set a flat $100,000 study fee for large loads in ERCOT in September 2026, with financial security posted separately.

faqs.question: What is a minimum bill in a data center electric service agreement?
faqs.answer: It is the amount the customer owes each month regardless of actual use, usually tied to a share of contract demand. The Berkeley Lab and Brattle review found a median minimum billing demand of 80% of contract demand. AEP Ohio's data center tariff sets it at up to 85% of contract capacity.

faqs.question: Can a will-serve letter be transferred when the land is sold?
faqs.answer: Only if the utility agrees. Letters, study positions and security are usually tied to the requesting customer and load. Get written confirmation from the utility that it will honor them for the buyer before you rely on them in price.

faqs.question: How does Invariant check a site's power documents?
faqs.answer: Invariant places every power document on an evidence ladder, from map proximity up to an executed agreement or metered service, and confirms with the utility where possible. Sites are tiered by that evidence before any parcel work or introduction.

title: Texas data center power in 2026: SB 6, ERCOT Batch Zero and what they mean for site selection
description: How SB 6, the PUCT's large load rule, ERCOT's Batch Zero study and the 2026 energization pause change the value of Texas data center sites with real power.
intro: A data center that needs 75 MW or more from the ERCOT grid can't get approval to energize in Texas as of November 2026. Senate Bill 6 set new terms for large loads in 2025. The PUCT turned them into a rule in September 2026: a $100,000 study fee, $50,000 per MW of security and a long list of disclosures. ERCOT moved pending requests into a single Batch Zero study and, on August 3, 2026, stopped approving energization of new data center and crypto loads of 75 MW or more. The practical result for site selection is simple. Capacity that is already energized or classified is worth more than it was a year ago, and a substation map is worth less.
takeaways: SB 6 applies to new or expanded ERCOT loads of 75 MW and up, and the PUCT's §25.194 rule now requires a $100,000 study fee and $50,000 per MW of security before any study.
ERCOT's Batch Zero replaced one-by-one studies. Of about 474 GW in the queue, roughly 194 GW was conditionally classified and 302.2 GW excluded.
Since August 3, 2026, ERCOT has not approved energization of new data centers or crypto loads of 75 MW or more, and since September 21 TCEQ has paused data center permits statewide.
El Paso, the Panhandle and parts of East Texas are outside ERCOT and run on their own utility tariffs, but the permit pause still applies there.

sections.heading: What Senate Bill 6 changed for loads of 75 MW and up

blocks.text: Senate Bill 6 was signed in June 2025 and took effect immediately. It rewrote the terms on which large loads connect to the ERCOT grid. The trigger is a new or expanded interconnection at a single site above a demand threshold the Public Utility Commission of Texas (PUCT) sets at 75 MW, unless the PUCT finds a lower number is needed.
The statute does six things a site buyer has to price in:

items: Disclosure of duplicate requests. A customer must say whether it is pursuing a substantially similar interconnection request elsewhere in Texas that would change, delay or withdraw this one.
A study fee of at least $100,000 for the initial transmission screening, credited toward later obligations at the same site.
Site control, shown through ownership, a lease or another legal interest the PUCT accepts.
Uniform financial commitments, which can include per-MW security, contributions in aid of construction or advance payment for equipment.

Curtailment during firm load shed. Loads interconnected after December 31, 2025 must be curtailable under a protocol the utility develops with ERCOT, with the equipment needed to do it. Weil's summary calls it a remote kill switch for grid emergencies.

Review of co-location with existing generation. A net-metering arrangement between a new large load and a generator registered as stand-alone on September 1, 2025 goes to ERCOT for a study within 120 days and then to the PUCT, which has 60 days to approve, deny or add conditions.

blocks.text: SB 6 also created a competitively procured demand reduction program for loads of 75 MW or more and requires disclosure of on-site backup generation that can carry at least half the site's demand. ERCOT can direct that backup generation to run in an emergency.

blocks.text: The PUCT tracks its SB 6 work in Project No. 58317. Its September 22, 2026 status report lists the projects below. The one that matters most for site value is 16 TAC §25.194, the large load interconnection standard, adopted at the September 18, 2026 open meeting.

blocks.text: Under §25.194, a large load customer has to sign an intermediate agreement before ERCOT will include it in an interconnection study. It pays a $100,000 study fee and posts $50,000 per MW of requested peak demand as security. Expansions count too: a site already above 75 MW that adds 75 MW or more is treated as a new request for the increment. The disclosures go well beyond the statute. The customer must report the type of site control (a signed purchase or lease option counts, and a lease option must run at least five years), any substantially similar request with its ERCOT serial number and size, water volumes, backup generation, how it plans to buy power and whether it will register as a controllable load resource.

The duplicate-request rule has a hard definition. A request elsewhere counts as material if approving it would delay this project by a year or more, change its peak demand by 20% or more, or move its point of interconnection. That ends the habit of filing the same campus at four substations and keeping the best answer.

sections.heading: ERCOT replaced one-by-one studies with Batch Zero

blocks.text: Until July 2026, transmission providers studied each large load on its own under ERCOT's Large Load Interconnection Study (LLIS) process. That process closed to new reviews on July 10, 2026. The PUCT approved its replacement, Planning Guide Revision Request 145 and Nodal Protocol Revision Request 1325, on June 18, 2026.

Batch Zero is a one-time, system-wide study of every qualifying load. It sorts each load into one of two groups. A Base Load already energized, sat in a quarterly stability assessment by May 1, 2026, or holds a complete and validated prior study. It is modeled as background and gets no new MW allocation. A Studied Load had enough maturity to get in but still needs an allocation. It receives a Low Power Consumption amount it can draw firm, and it can only go higher by registering as a Provisional Controllable Load Resource and following ERCOT dispatch. There is also a bring-your-own-generation path, the Withdrawal-Limited Private Use Network, which caps net draw at the point of interconnection. A load that qualifies for neither group can't get approval for initial energization and waits for a future batch.

The numbers explain why. ERCOT told the Texas Senate on July 29, 2026 that it was tracking about 474 GW of large loads seeking interconnection as of June, about 90% of them data centers. Only about 205 GW had a study that qualified for Batch Zero. On September 3, ERCOT gave transmission providers conditional classifications. 204 projects totaling 66.4 GW conditionally qualified as base load, 158 projects totaling 127.9 GW as studied load, and 373 projects totaling 302.2 GW were excluded. Eleven projects elected the bring-your-own-generation path.

Geography is uneven. Dallas and Harris counties lead conditional base load at roughly 5.7 GW each. Cameron, Jones and Childress counties show up near the top once studied load is added, which means the next wave is aimed well outside the metro substations.

sections.heading: The August 2026 energization pause and the September permit pause

blocks.text: On August 3, 2026, Governor Abbott directed the PUCT and ERCOT to complete a verification and audit of every data center moving through the interconnection process before letting it proceed. ERCOT acted the same day. It paused the Batch Zero study, delayed final classification of all large loads and stopped approving energization for data centers and crypto mining facilities of 75 MW or more. The pause hits loads that are not yet connected. Loads already on the system keep running.

Two reviews are now running. The eligibility verification checks the attestations behind each Batch Zero load. ERCOT's July deck listed the evidence it expects: purchase orders for long-lead equipment, real estate agreements, land use approvals, end-user agreements and construction contracts. A separate community impact review covers data centers and crypto loads of 25 MW and up, including the 25 to 75 MW band that sits below the Batch Zero threshold. ERCOT said it would file both reports with the PUCT by December 10, 2026 and give final Batch Zero inclusion in December. It hasn't said how far the study will slip past its original April 9, 2027 deadline.

On September 21, 2026, the Governor told the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality to stop issuing permits sought by data centers until the audits finish, and said no state agency should advance data center approvals in the meantime. That covers every permit a data center seeks from TCEQ, which includes air permits for backup generators. TCEQ had to report its compliance by October 19, 2026. No end date has been published.

So, as of November 2026, a 75 MW data center in ERCOT that is not already energized cannot get energization approval, cannot get a TCEQ permit and cannot know its Batch Zero allocation until at least December.

sections.heading: Texas outside ERCOT runs on different rules

blocks.text: ERCOT carries about 90% of Texas electric load. El Paso and Far West Texas sit in the Western Interconnection. The Panhandle and parts of East Texas sit in the Eastern Interconnection. Batch Zero and ERCOT's energization pause are ERCOT processes, so they don't govern El Paso Electric, Southwestern Public Service (Xcel) in the Panhandle, Entergy Texas around Beaumont or SWEPCO in Northeast Texas. Weil's reading of SB 6 also frames its interconnection and curtailment provisions around the ERCOT region.

These utilities are writing their own large load terms. SPS filed a large load tariff at the PUCT on October 5, 2026 (Docket 60332) for customers of 75 MW and up. It would let a large load meet its demand through dedicated generation, including third-party generation contracted through SPS or customer-owned generation.

Two cautions. The TCEQ permit pause applies to data center projects anywhere in Texas, so leaving ERCOT doesn't get a project its air permit. And a smaller utility's will-serve letter still needs the same reading as any other: what transmission it assumes, what it costs the customer and what date it supports.

blocks.text: Power was already the scarce input in Texas. Paces' November 2025 analysis of ERCOT found that only about 17% of substations near land suitable for data centers had positive withdrawal capacity. The 2026 rules add a second filter. A site's value now depends on where its load sits in the Batch Zero classification and whether it has already energized.

We grade Texas sites on a five-rung power evidence ladder. Rung 0 is a map. Rung 1 is proximity to a line or substation of the right voltage. Rung 2 is a named MW figure at a named station from a utility or planning record. blocks.text: Before any parcel work, kill the disqualifiers. Is the site already claimed or operating? Under option? Listed? Owned by a buyer of environmental liabilities? Coal ash or contamination? A county moratorium? Then ask for the documents behind the power claim: the ERCOT classification notice, the security posting confirmation from the transmission provider, the intermediate agreement and the duplicate-request disclosure. Invariant screens Texas sites this way before any introduction, and sorts them into tier A (documented power), tier B (a named power path with a date) and tier C (land near capacity).

faqs.question: Did ERCOT stop approving new data centers in 2026?
faqs.answer: ERCOT paused approvals to energize data centers and crypto mining facilities of 75 MW or more on August 3, 2026, after a directive from Governor Abbott. Loads already connected were not affected. ERCOT said it would file its verification report by December 10, 2026.

faqs.question: What does a large load have to pay to enter an ERCOT interconnection study?
faqs.answer: Under 16 TAC §25.194, adopted September 18, 2026, the customer signs an intermediate agreement, pays a $100,000 study fee and posts $50,000 per MW of requested peak demand as financial security. It also has to file disclosures on site control, duplicate requests, water, backup generation and power supply.

faqs.question: What is ERCOT Batch Zero?
faqs.answer: Batch Zero is a one-time, system-wide study of qualifying large loads that replaced ERCOT's one-by-one Large Load Interconnection Study process in July 2026. Loads are classified as base load or studied load, and studied loads get a firm draw limit plus an option to consume more under ERCOT dispatch.

faqs.question: How big is the ERCOT large load queue?
faqs.answer: ERCOT reported about 474 GW of large loads seeking interconnection as of June 2026, roughly 90% data centers. Its September conditional classification put about 194 GW in Batch Zero and excluded 302.2 GW.

faqs.question: Can a data center avoid the ERCOT pause by locating in El Paso or the Panhandle?
faqs.answer: Those areas are outside ERCOT, so Batch Zero and ERCOT's energization pause don't govern them, and SPS has filed its own large load tariff. The September 2026 TCEQ permit pause applies to data center projects statewide, though.

faqs.question: How does Invariant check a Texas site's power claim?
faqs.answer: Invariant places the claim on a power evidence ladder and asks for the document behind it, such as the Batch Zero classification, the security posting or the executed agreement. Sites are screened for disqualifiers and graded before any introduction.

title: Retired power plant sites for data centers: what transfers and what can sink the deal
description: Retired coal and gas plant sites offer switchyards, water and zoning, but a generator's export right is not a load right. What transfers, and the coal ash risks.
intro: A retired coal or gas plant is one of the best places to look for data center power, because the switchyard, transmission lines, water and heavy industrial zoning are already there. What does not come with the site is the right to draw power. The plant's interconnection let it push energy onto the grid. A data center needs a withdrawal right from the utility and the grid operator, and that has to be studied and granted again. Buy for the infrastructure, verify the load path separately, and price the coal ash before you price the land.
takeaways: A plant's generator interconnection is an export right. Load service for a data center needs its own utility study and agreement.
PJM and MISO let replacement generation reuse a retiring unit's rights on fixed terms, and FERC's 2025 and 2026 orders set PJM's co-location rules.
Coal ash units, groundwater findings and recorded covenants decide how many acres are actually buildable.
Find candidates in EIA-860M retirements, then confirm the unit stopped and check the owner before any parcel work.

sections.heading: What a retired plant site brings to a data center

blocks.text: A coal or gas plant was sited for the same things a large data center needs. It sits on a high-voltage switchyard with lines that once carried hundreds of megawatts, sometimes more than a gigawatt, out to the grid. It usually has a cooling water intake and the permits behind it. The land is zoned and taxed as heavy industrial, the neighbors are used to a large facility, and many sites have a rail spur and a gas lateral. None of that guarantees power for a new load, but it puts the site on a different rung of evidence than a farm field three miles from a substation.

Homer City in Pennsylvania is the public example most people cite. The former coal station, once the largest in the state, is being redeveloped as a 3,200-acre campus with up to 4.5 GW of gas generation from seven GE Vernova turbines, and the developers said much of the critical infrastructure was already in place from the legacy plant. FracTracker documented demolition blasts and the start of vertical construction there in April 2026.

Notice what that project did. It did not plug a data center into the old plant's grid connection. It built new generation on site. That choice says a lot about how interconnection rights work, which is the subject of the next section.

Owners are also changing hands with data centers in mind. In March 2026 a data center developer announced a deal to buy the Morgantown Generating Station in Maryland, whose coal units shut in 2022 while four smaller oil-fired units still run. The acquisition needed FERC approval, and the buyer had not said how power would be generated.

sections.heading: A generator interconnection is not a load connection

blocks.text: This is where most retired-plant pitches go wrong. A power plant holds an interconnection agreement that lets it inject energy at a point on the transmission system. In PJM the deliverable part of that right is called Capacity Interconnection Rights. A data center needs the opposite: the right to withdraw energy, which comes from transmission service and retail service from the local utility. A 1,000 MW export right does not become a 1,000 MW load right when the boilers go cold.

The grid studies are different too. A plant's interconnection study asked whether the network could carry its output away under stress. A load study asks whether the network can deliver power in, often during the same peak hours. The answer at the same bus can be very different. The physical assets help a lot: the switchyard, the breakers, the line rights of way. The paper right to withdraw has to be earned again through the utility's large-load process.

FERC addressed this directly for PJM. In its December 18, 2025 order in Docket EL25-49, the Commission found PJM's tariff unjust and unreasonable because it lacked clear rates, terms and conditions for co-located load, meaning load connected behind or next to a generator. It directed PJM to spell out how generators can use provisional interconnection service, service below nameplate and Surplus Interconnection Service to serve co-located load. It also said an existing generator cannot withdraw its capacity from the system to start serving a co-located load until the network upgrades needed to keep existing customers reliable are in service, with the generator paying the full cost.

On June 18, 2026, in EL25-49-002, FERC largely sustained that order on rehearing and accepted rates, terms and conditions for three transmission services for co-located load: Interim Network Integration Transmission Service, Firm Contract Demand and Non-Firm Contract Demand. It also required more compliance changes, including a load-based materiality threshold for behind-the-meter generation. As of November 2026, treat the PJM co-location rules as still being finished through compliance filings and check the docket before relying on a specific term.

For a buyer, the practical reading is short. Co-location at an operating plant is a path with rules now. Co-location at a retired plant usually means new generation, a new or replacement interconnection, and a transmission service election for the load. A retired plant's old agreement is evidence of what the bus once carried. It is not a service commitment for your campus.

sections.heading: How ISOs let a site reuse its interconnection

blocks.text: The grid operators have built paths that let new generation reuse an old plant's injection rights faster than a fresh queue position. These are generator rules. They matter to a data center when the plan includes on-site or adjacent generation, as at Homer City.

PJM's generator replacement process took effect January 30, 2026 after FERC accepted a revised filing on January 29, 2026. It lets a replacement resource take over a deactivating unit's Capacity Interconnection Rights through an expedited study, if the new resource connects at the same substation, runs at the same voltage and does not exceed the retiring unit's maximum output. Under PJM's existing rules a deactivated unit keeps its CIRs for one year, so the clock starts at deactivation.

MISO has run a generator replacement process since 2019. Utility Dive reported in April 2025 that about 5.9 GW of replacement requests had been approved and 4.9 GW were under study, and that replacements generally have to connect at the same point as the retiring unit. MISO had asked FERC to allow an electrically equivalent point instead. Check the current MISO tariff for the status of that change.

Both processes are built around the owner of the retiring unit. A buyer of the land alone, without the generating assets and the interconnection agreement, should not assume it can use them. Ask who holds the agreement, whether it has been assigned, and how many months remain before the rights lapse.

A retirement date is also not final until the unit stops. Since May 2025 the Department of Energy has used Federal Power Act section 202(c) emergency orders to keep plants that were scheduled to retire available to run. J.H. Campbell in Michigan, slated to close May 31, 2025, was under a 90-day order running to November 14, 2026, and DOE's 2026 list also covers units including Eddystone in Pennsylvania, Centralia in Washington and Craig in Colorado. A site whose plant is under a 202(c) order cannot be demolished or repurposed on the schedule the seller describes.

blocks.text: Rank what you collect on a simple ladder. A map showing the plant is rung 0. Proximity to a high-voltage switchyard is rung 1. A retired plant's documented export level at a named station is rung 2, the same rung as a broker's "500 MW available". A utility study for your load is rung 3. An executed service or interconnection agreement with a date, or energized and metered service, is rung 4. Most retired plant sites sit on rung 2 when they first reach a buyer, and that's fine as long as everyone says so.

sections.heading: Coal ash and other liabilities that can sink the deal

blocks.text: Coal ash is the item that kills the most coal plant reuse plans, because it rarely leaves the site. EPA's 2015 CCR rule set national requirements for ash landfills and surface impoundments, including groundwater monitoring, corrective action for releases, closure and a public website where each facility posts its compliance records. The May 8, 2024 legacy rule extended coverage to inactive impoundments at inactive plants and added requirements for CCR management units, meaning ash placed outside regulated units, such as old fill areas.

The schedule has moved since then. A final rule published February 10, 2026 extended several legacy-rule deadlines. Groundwater monitoring systems at affected units are now due February 10, 2031 instead of May 8, 2028. Closure and post-closure care plans are due August 11, 2031, and closure must start by February 9, 2032. The first part of the facility evaluation report moved to February 9, 2027. The 2024 rule is also under challenge in the D.C. Circuit, a case the notice describes as in abeyance, and EPA has said it plans to reconsider the rule.

EPA has more changes in progress. In November 2025 it proposed moving the closure deadline for certain unlined impoundments over 40 acres from October 17, 2028 to October 17, 2031, and in April 2026 it proposed further amendments to the Part 257 rules. Neither was shown as final on EPA's page when we checked in November 2026.

Longer deadlines do not shrink the liability. They mean the investigation that tells you how much ash is in the ground, and whether it is reaching the aquifer, may not happen until years after you buy. Get the facility's CCR website records yourself. Read the closure method: closure in place leaves capped ash and decades of post-closure care, often in the middle of what a site plan shows as buildable acres.

Then look at the paper on the land. Closed ash units and remediated areas usually come with recorded environmental covenants that limit groundwater use, bar residential use, require access for monitoring wells, or prohibit digging through a cap. Those restrictions run with the land and can block a building pad, a duct bank or a stormwater pond. Pull the title commitment early, not at the end.

Check who owns the plant. Some retired plants are bought by firms whose business is taking on environmental liability: they acquire the site, run the remediation and demolition, and resell parcels later. That owner may be a good counterparty, but it controls the timing, it often keeps the ash units, and its deed may carve out the parts of the site with the most electrical value. Put it on the kill sheet as a question before parcel work starts.

Demolition is its own budget line. Older boiler houses and turbine halls often contain asbestos. EPA's asbestos NESHAP requires a thorough inspection before demolition, notice to the delegated agency, and work practices such as wetting regulated material and sealing it in leak-tight containers. Find out who has already done that work and who pays for what remains.

sections.heading: How to find retired plant sites worth screening

blocks.text: Start with EIA. The EIA-860M monthly generator inventory tracks existing and proposed units at plants of 1 MW and up, and since March 2017 data it has included a tab of generators retired since 2002. The October 2026 file came out October 23, and the next is scheduled for November 24, 2026. Filter for coal and gas steam units by state, sum retired nameplate capacity by plant, and keep the plant ID so you can join it to other records.

items: Sort plants by retired capacity at a single site, then check whether any units at the same plant still run.
Cross-check the DOE 202(c) list and the ISO deactivation records to confirm the unit really stopped.
Open the CCR public website for each coal plant before visiting. No website at a coal plant is itself a question.
Look up current owner and recent transfers in county records, and flag liability buyers.
Check for announced redevelopment, options and listings so you don't spend time on a site already claimed.
Search the county for data center moratoria or zoning text changes.

blocks.text: That order matters. Power evidence first, then the disqualifiers, then parcels. A plant that survives gets a tier: A when there is documented power for a new load, B when there is a named power path with a date, such as a replacement filing or a utility load study under way, and C when it is land next to capacity with nothing yet on paper. Invariant screens retired plant sites this way before any introduction, and most of them land in B or C until the utility puts a number in writing.

faqs.question: Can a data center use a retired power plant's interconnection?
faqs.answer: Not directly. A plant's interconnection agreement lets it inject power, while a data center needs to withdraw power through utility and transmission service. The switchyard and lines help, but the load still needs its own study and service agreement.

faqs.question: What is co-location in PJM?
faqs.answer: Co-location means a large load connected at or next to a generator. FERC's December 2025 order required PJM to set clear rules for it, and a June 2026 order accepted three transmission services for co-located load: Interim NITS, Firm Contract Demand and Non-Firm Contract Demand. Compliance filings were still refining the rules in 2026.

faqs.question: How long do interconnection rights last after a plant retires in PJM?
faqs.answer: Under PJM's rules a deactivated unit keeps its Capacity Interconnection Rights for one year. The replacement process that took effect January 30, 2026 lets a new resource at the same substation and voltage, no larger than the retired unit, use those rights through an expedited study.

faqs.question: Is coal ash a deal breaker for a data center site?
faqs.answer: Not always, but it often takes the best acres. Closed-in-place ash units come with post-closure care and recorded land-use limits, and EPA's 2026 extension pushed groundwater monitoring at legacy units to 2031. Read the facility's CCR website records before any parcel work.

faqs.question: Where can I find a list of retired power plants?
faqs.answer: EIA's monthly EIA-860M inventory includes a tab of generators retired since 2002, with plant IDs that link to other records. Cross-check it against DOE's 202(c) orders, since some plants scheduled to retire are being kept available to run.

faqs.question: How does Invariant evaluate retired plant sites?
faqs.answer: Invariant starts from the power evidence at the station, removes sites with disqualifiers such as coal ash, liability owners or existing claims, and only then looks at parcels. Each surviving site gets a tier based on the documents behind its power.

title: Converting a bitcoin mining site to AI or HPC: what carries over and what you rebuild
description: Converting a bitcoin mining site to an AI or HPC data center: what carries over, what you rebuild, power contract checks and a site evaluation checklist.
intro: An energized bitcoin mining site gives an AI or HPC buyer the scarce part of a data center: a utility connection that already exists. The substation, the service agreement, the metered load history and the land usually carry over. The facility mostly does not. Expect to rebuild for redundancy, backup generation, liquid cooling, fiber and a hardened shell, and expect to renegotiate power terms, because mining loads are often built around curtailment while an AI tenant needs firm service. Evaluate the contract first, then the building.
takeaways: The utility connection, substation and land are the assets; most mining buildings and electrical systems get rebuilt or demolished.
Read the power contract for curtailment and interruptible terms before pricing a lease, since AI tenants need firm service.
In Texas, check Load Resource status, SB 6 curtailment rules and whether the new load needs a Batch Zero study.
Small 2 to 10 MW mining sites suit inference and edge deployments, not large training clusters.

sections.heading: Why energized mining sites are being converted

blocks.text: An AI or HPC buyer can wait years for a new large-load connection. A mining site that is already energized has the one thing that queue can't sell: a working utility connection with a known capacity and a metered history. Paces' 2025 analysis of ERCOT's 2028 summer-peak planning case found that only about 17% of substations near viable data center sites had positive withdrawal headroom. Land near a substation is common. Spare capacity at that substation is not.

The public miners have moved first. Core Scientific's 10-Q for the quarter ended September 30, 2026 describes a strategic shift from mining for its own account to high-density colocation, with CoreWeave leases on 12-year initial terms and a second set of leases with AMD and a neocloud counterparty for about 530 MW of critical IT capacity across five of its sites. TeraWulf announced in August 2025 that Fluidstack's contracted critical IT load at its Lake Mariner campus in western New York had reached about 360 MW, with a Google backstop of about $3.2 billion. IREN signed an agreement with Microsoft on November 2, 2025 to provide GPU services at its Childress, Texas facilities, valued at about $9.7 billion over an average five-year term.

Read those filings closely and a pattern shows up. The power and the land carried over. Most of the rest was rebuilt, and some of it was torn down. Bitfarms' plan for its 18 MW former mining site near Moses Lake, Washington, filed with the city in January 2026, calls for demolishing the existing mining facility before building a liquid-cooled HPC and AI data center.

sections.heading: What carries over from a mining site

blocks.text: The utility service is the asset. That means the substation, the transformers, the service voltage, the interconnection or electric service agreement, and the billing history that proves the load actually ran. On the power evidence ladder Invariant uses, an energized and metered site sits on the top rung. But it sits there for the load that was approved. A 50 MW mining load with a curtailment arrangement and an AI load that expects firm service are different requests, and the utility may treat the second one as a new study.

Land and site control usually carry over, along with whatever acreage was left for expansion. Some permits carry over too. Zoning that allowed a mining data center may or may not cover a building with a generator yard, cooling towers or dry coolers, and a larger fuel inventory. Check the use classification against the new design, not the old one.

items: Utility service, substation and transformers, subject to confirming their rating and age.
The interconnection or service agreement, after reading its curtailment, interruptibility and transfer terms.
Metered load history, which is the best evidence a buyer can get that the MW figure is real.
Land, easements and site control, including unused acreage for expansion.
Some local approvals, after checking them against the new equipment list.

blocks.text: Creative Strategies calls the interconnection agreement a starting point. Mining sites often hang off one or two transmission lines and a small number of substation transformers. That was fine for a load that could drop off the grid without losing revenue it couldn't recover.

sections.heading: Power contract terms: curtailment versus firm service

blocks.text: Many miners earn part of their margin by not running. In ERCOT, loads can take part in demand response by offering directly into the market or by cutting usage when wholesale prices rise, and a load or aggregation of loads can qualify through a QSE to provide ancillary services as a Load Resource. ERCOT also runs Emergency Response Service for loads that respond during grid emergencies. A Controllable Load Resource is a load that can raise or lower consumption to help hold grid frequency.

An AI training cluster or a hosted inference platform does not want any of that. The tenant is paying for capacity it can use every hour. So the first document to pull is the power contract, and the first question is whether the site's MW figure assumed interruptible service. If the miner registered as a Load Resource, enrolled in a curtailment program, or bought power on a structure that depended on dropping load during peaks, that structure has to be unwound or replaced before a tenant signs.

Texas added a second layer in 2025. Senate Bill 6 treats loads of at least 75 MW as large loads, with the PUCT able to set a lower threshold. Large loads interconnected after December 31, 2025 must have equipment that lets ERCOT curtail them directly during firm load shed. Customers must disclose whether they keep on-site backup generation equal to at least half of the proposed load, and ERCOT can direct those customers to deploy that generation or curtail during an energy emergency. SB 6 also directs the PUCT and ERCOT to build a competitively procured demand reduction service for large loads.

As of November 2026, ERCOT is running large-load interconnections of 75 MW or more through its Batch Zero study process under PGRR145, with 2026 deadlines for attestations and load information forms. If a conversion changes the load type, the ramp or the total MW at a site, ask the interconnecting utility in writing whether the request falls inside Batch Zero or needs a new study. Outside Texas the mechanics differ, but the question is the same: was this service approved as firm or as interruptible, and what does the utility need to change it?

sections.heading: What you rebuild for an AI or HPC tenant

blocks.text: Ramboll's mission critical team lists what a crypto facility typically lacks for AI use: building reliability, backup power, cooling capacity, and redundancy in power and cooling. Creative Strategies puts numbers on the cooling gap. Mining racks run around 10 kW on air. Liquid cooling becomes necessary above roughly 30 to 40 kW per rack, and current AI racks run well past that.

Uptime commitments drive most of the rebuild. Uptime Institute defines Tier III as concurrently maintainable, meaning no shutdowns for equipment replacement and maintenance, and Tier IV as fault tolerant, where an individual equipment failure or path interruption does not reach IT operations. A mining hall has no reason to meet either. A colocation lease with service credits does.

blocks.text: Fiber is the gap that surprises people. A mining site can run on one modest connection because hashing sends little data. Training clusters need high-bandwidth links out of the site, and inference needs low latency to users. Remote sites with no metro fiber nearby may need new diverse routes before any tenant will look at them.

Then there is the money. Creative Strategies estimates AI-grade capex at roughly $6 million to $13 million per MW, against a few hundred thousand dollars per MW for mining, and notes that this usually needs an investment-grade tenant or a well-capitalized AI cloud operator on a long commitment. The public deals show it: TeraWulf's Lake Mariner leases came with a Google backstop of tenant obligations, and Core Scientific's CoreWeave leases run 12-year initial terms.

sections.heading: Small mining sites fit inference and edge, not training

blocks.text: Most of the US mining fleet isn't 300 MW campuses. Plenty of sites are 2 to 10 MW, often a few containers behind a single transformer at a substation or a gas field. Those sites are a poor match for frontier training, which wants hundreds of MW in one place with room to grow.

They can work for inference, rendering, smaller HPC jobs or edge deployments, where the buyer wants a few MW quickly and close to users or fiber. The questions shift. Distance to a metro and to carrier hotels matters more than total MW. Whether the utility will serve the same few MW as firm load matters more than expansion acreage. Be honest about the ceiling. A 5 MW site with no path to 50 MW will be priced as a 5 MW site.

Count the shrink as well. A mining site's MW figure is total utility capacity. After cooling overhead, redundancy and the loss of curtailment flexibility, the critical IT load an AI tenant can contract for is lower. Get the engineer's number for usable critical IT MW before quoting anything to a buyer.

sections.heading: Checklist for evaluating a mining site for conversion

blocks.text: Work through this before anyone prices a lease. Each line should end in a document, not an opinion.

items: Pull the electric service or interconnection agreement. Record the contracted MW, the service voltage, any interruptible or curtailment terms, and whether the agreement can be assigned or amended for a new use.
Get 12 to 24 months of interval meter data. Compare actual peak draw with the contracted figure.

In ERCOT, confirm whether the load is registered as a Load Resource or Controllable Load Resource, enrolled in Emergency Response Service, or subject to SB 6 curtailment requirements, and what it takes to exit.
Ask the utility in writing whether converting to firm data center load requires a new load study, and get the expected timeline.
Inventory the substation: transformer ratings, age, number of incoming lines, and whether a second source is feasible.
Have an engineer estimate usable critical IT MW after cooling and redundancy, for both N+1 and 2N designs.
Check zoning and air permitting against the new equipment list, including generators and fuel storage.
Map fiber: nearest long-haul and metro routes, carriers on site, and cost to build a diverse second path.
Assess the building honestly. Price a retrofit against demolition and a new shell.
Run the kill sheet: already under lease or option, publicly listed for sale, environmental liability, local moratorium.

sections.heading: How Invariant screens mining sites

blocks.text: Invariant treats a mining site as a power lead first. We rank it by the evidence behind the MW: a broker's capacity figure is a claim, a metered bill is proof that load ran, and an executed agreement for firm service at the new load is what a data center buyer needs. A site whose only path to firm power is a new study goes in the named-power-path tier with a date, not the documented-power tier. We check the contract terms and the kill list before anyone spends money on drawings, so a buyer sees what carries over and what they'll pay to rebuild before an introduction is made.

faqs.question: Can a bitcoin mining facility be converted into an AI data center?
faqs.answer: Yes, and several public miners are doing it, but the conversion usually keeps the power connection and land and replaces most of the facility. Core Scientific now describes high-density colocation as its business, while Bitfarms plans to demolish its 18 MW Moses Lake mining building before building a liquid-cooled AI facility.

faqs.question: What is the biggest difference between a mining site and an AI data center?
faqs.answer: Reliability. Mining can shut off when power is expensive or the grid is stressed, and many miners earn revenue doing so. AI tenants expect concurrently maintainable or fault tolerant facilities with backup power and firm utility service.

faqs.question: Does the interconnection agreement transfer when a mining site is converted?
faqs.answer: The physical connection stays, but the terms may not fit the new load. Read the agreement for curtailment, interruptible service and assignment clauses, and ask the utility in writing whether a change to firm data center load requires a new study. In ERCOT, loads of 75 MW or more currently go through the Batch Zero process.

faqs.question: How does Texas SB 6 affect converted mining sites?
faqs.answer: SB 6 sets a 75 MW large-load threshold and requires large loads interconnected after December 31, 2025 to have equipment that lets ERCOT curtail them during firm load shed. It also requires disclosure of backup generation equal to at least half the load. A converted site that triggers new interconnection review should plan for these rules.

faqs.question: Are small 5 MW mining sites useful for AI?
faqs.answer: Usually for inference, edge or smaller HPC work rather than training. The deciding factors are firm service from the utility, fiber and distance to users, not total MW. Invariant screens small sites for those factors before suggesting them to a buyer.

title: Behind-the-meter power for data centers: when on-site gas works and what to verify
description: How on-site gas turbines, engines and fuel cells can power a data center before the grid arrives, and the gas, air permit, equipment and regulatory checks to run first.
intro: An on-site gas plant can make a data center site work when the grid date is years away, but only if four things line up: firm gas supply, an air permit sized for the whole campus, generation equipment with a real delivery slot, and a regulatory structure that lets the power reach the load. Verify each with a document. A pipeline on a map or a broker's "gas available" line is not that evidence. This guide covers what recent projects show, how the main BTM configurations compare and what to ask for on each.
takeaways: Treat a BTM site as four approvals on four clocks: gas, air, equipment and regulation.
Ask the pipeline for firm capacity, pressure and gas quality in writing before any equipment order.
Get the emissions calculation for the full build-out, since phased minor permits draw aggregation challenges.
Plan the grid path from day one so the bridge generation has an end state.

sections.heading: Why buyers are pricing sites with their own generation

blocks.text: The grid answer at most good substations is a date several years out. Paces looked at ERCOT substations that had suitable land nearby and found only about 17% showed positive withdrawal capacity, meaning room to add load without making existing overloads worse. That is one market and one method, but it matches what site selectors hear from utilities across the country.

Behind-the-meter (BTM) generation is the workaround. The site makes its own power from gas turbines, reciprocating engines or fuel cells, either for the whole load or as a bridge until utility service arrives. Small modular reactors come up in every pitch deck. Treat them as a later-decade option. None of the sources below rely on one for first power.

A BTM site doesn't remove the power question. It moves it. Instead of asking whether the utility has headroom, you are asking whether the gas, the air permit, the turbines and the regulator will all line up by the same date. Each of those can fail on its own schedule.

sections.heading: What recent on-site gas projects show

blocks.text: xAI's Colossus site in Memphis is the case everyone cites. SELC says xAI began operating there in June 2024 using as many as 35 unpermitted gas turbines, removed them after a Clean Air Act notice of intent to sue, and obtained permits for the remaining 15. The permits came after the turbines were already running, which is the order of operations a lender or tenant will ask about.

The fight then moved across the state line. In April 2026 SELC and Earthjustice sued on behalf of the NAACP over 27 turbines, up to 495 MW, at xAI's Southaven, Mississippi facility. As of November 2026 we have not seen a final ruling. The lesson for a buyer is plain: installing turbines faster than the permit record creates litigation risk that can outlast the speed advantage.

Stargate in Abilene took a different route. Floodlight and The Texas Tribune report the developers built 10 gas turbines and 62 backup diesel generators under minor Texas permits, with a 360 MW on-site gas plant, then applied for a major air permit to add 41 more turbines and 18 more generators. Crusoe describes the turbines as backup, though the permits allow continuous use. A former EPA enforcement chief quoted in the piece argued the project should have been permitted as one source.

Homer City, Pennsylvania, is the brownfield version. The developers announced up to 4.5 GW of gas generation on the 3,200-acre former coal plant site, seven GE Vernova turbines with first deliveries expected in 2026, gas from the Texas Eastern system about five miles away, and existing ties to PJM and NYISO. The coal unit, 1,884 MW, shut in mid-2023. Reuse of a retired plant site gave the project an existing grid connection and an industrial land use to build on.

Two utility-led models sit at the other end. In Ohio, PUCO approved AEP Ohio's on-site fuel cell project for AWS and Cologix data centers, with the customers covering full project cost and the fuel cells described as a way to start operating while the grid expands. In Louisiana, regulators approved Entergy's three gas plants, about 2.3 GW, for Meta's Richland Parish campus. That is gas built for one customer but owned by the utility and delivered through the grid, so it is a front-of-meter deal with different risks.
