sections.heading: Verify gas supply before anything else

blocks.text: A pipeline on the map is rung 1 evidence. It says nothing about whether that line has capacity at the pressure you need. Ask the pipeline operator, in writing, for available firm capacity at the nearest interconnect, the required lateral length and who builds it, the delivery pressure, and the gas quality spec. Turbine and fuel cell vendors publish fuel requirements. Check heating value and contaminants against them before an equipment order, not after.

Firm transport matters more than commodity price. An islanded campus with interruptible gas has no backstop on a cold day when residential demand takes priority. Price the firm transport contract and its term. Ask whether dual fuel or on-site storage is part of the design, and how many hours of operation it covers.

The Permian shows the other side of the problem. Waha hub prices were negative for a record 25 straight days by March 12, 2026, because pipelines could not move the gas out. Cheap gas at the wellhead is why operators pitch data centers on mineral and gas acreage in West Texas, eastern New Mexico and the Plains states. Takeaway relief was expected mainly in the second half of 2026, so a site that depends on stranded gas pricing should model what happens once new pipes narrow that discount.

For acreage sites, confirm who holds the mineral rights and the surface rights, whether they are severed, and whether drilling or pipeline easements limit where buildings can go. A gas producer as landlord can be a strong supply partner. It can also mean your fuel price is tied to one counterparty.

sections.heading: Air permits, water and local opposition

blocks.text: Air permitting sets the real size of an on-site plant. Under EPA's Title V program, a major source is one with the potential to emit 100 tons per year of any air pollutant, 10 tons per year of a single hazardous air pollutant, or 25 tons per year of combined HAPs. Thresholds drop in ozone nonattainment areas, as low as 10 tons per year of NOx in extreme areas. Major new sources in attainment areas also face Prevention of Significant Deterioration review, which requires best available control technology and public involvement.

Floodlight found that more than half of the Texas data centers it reviewed reported NOx estimates just under the thresholds that trigger fuller review, such as 249.1 or 99.8 tons per year. That is legal when the numbers are real. It also invites the aggregation argument raised at Abilene: regulators or opponents can claim that phased minor permits are one major project. Ask for the emissions calculation for the full campus, not phase one.

Read the local record too. In both Memphis and Southaven, a notice of intent to sue came before the permit question was settled. Pull the air agency's comment docket for any nearby generation permit and check county minutes for opposition that has already organized.

Water gets missed. Combined cycle plants and some turbine inlet cooling designs need water, and a dry-cooled design costs output on hot days. Get the water source in writing: municipal allocation, groundwater permit or rights, or a reuse contract. Homer City's developers pointed to their own water supply as part of the pitch.

sections.heading: Equipment lead times, redundancy and cost

blocks.text: Large gas turbines are the long pole. GE Vernova reported 116 GW of gas equipment backlog and slot reservations at the end of the second quarter of 2026, up from 83 GW at the end of 2025. It is booking reservations about four to five years out and taking slots for 2031 delivery. A seller who says turbines are available should show a reservation agreement with a delivery quarter.

Smaller aeroderivative units and reciprocating engines are often quoted on shorter timelines, and the secondary market for used units is active. Get dated quotes. Lead times in this market have moved quarter to quarter.

An islanded data center has no grid to fall back on, so redundancy is part of the generation design. Size for N+1 at minimum on the generating units, and decide how you'll handle a gas supply outage, a failed transformer and planned maintenance. Grid-parallel operation lowers that burden but brings an interconnection agreement, protection studies and the utility's standby or backup service terms back into scope.

On cost, Lazard's 2026 analysis puts unsubsidized gas combined cycle at $51 to $129 per MWh and gas peaking at $144 to $276 per MWh. Those are utility-scale figures. Small on-site turbines and engines usually run closer to peaker economics than combined cycle, and the result swings with gas price and capacity factor. Lazard also points to a 15-year high in gas LCOE and long development lead times.

blocks.text: Two sites in our inventory pair on-site gas with a grid path, which is the structure most buyers ask about.

sections.heading: Regulatory treatment and the path to the grid

blocks.text: Who is allowed to sell power to whom is a state question. In many states, a third party selling electricity to a data center on the same site can look like a retail sale inside a utility's service territory. Self-generation by the load owner is usually treated differently. Get a short opinion from state utility counsel before structuring a developer-owned plant that sells to a tenant.

Texas is the clearest example of new rules. SB 6, signed June 20, 2025, requires ERCOT study and PUCT approval when a new large load sets up a net metering arrangement with an existing generator, with exemptions such as a parent company holding a majority interest in the generator as of January 1, 2025. It also requires large loads to disclose on-site backup generation in their interconnection requests, and lets ERCOT direct qualifying new loads to switch to backup generation during an emergency.

The PUCT adopted the implementing net metering rule, 16 TAC 25.205, on March 26, 2026. ERCOT revised its notice form on July 31, 2026, for loads of 75 MW or more seeking such an arrangement. If a Texas site plan depends on taking power from an existing plant, ask whether the review applies, whether it has been filed and what conditions came back.

Plan the grid path even for a site that starts islanded. Long-term, the grid gives you a backstop and possibly an export route. Ask the utility for a load study now so the queue clock starts, and record whether the bridge generators will stay as backup, move to another site or be sold. AEP's Ohio fuel cells were approved explicitly as a bridge while the grid expands.

Apply the same evidence ladder used for grid sites. Proximity to a pipeline is rung 1. A pipeline operator's written capacity figure at a named interconnect is rung 2. A firm transport agreement, a filed or issued air permit covering the full build-out and a turbine reservation are rung 3. Executed contracts with dates and units on site are rung 4. A broker's "gas available" claim is rung 1 until the pipeline letter is in hand.

Then run the kill sheet before parcel work. Drop sites already claimed or operating, sites in an air district where the full build-out cannot be permitted, and sites with organized opposition to an existing generation permit. Invariant screens BTM sites this way before any introduction, and grades them A for documented gas and permit evidence, B for a named supply path with a date, and C for land near a pipeline.

faqs.question: What does behind-the-meter power mean for a data center?
faqs.answer: It means the data center uses electricity generated on its own side of the utility meter, usually from on-site gas turbines, engines or fuel cells. It can run fully islanded or alongside a grid connection. The site still needs gas supply, an air permit and equipment, so it has its own approvals.

faqs.question: How long does it take to get gas turbines for a data center?
faqs.answer: For large gas turbines, GE Vernova was booking reservations about four to five years out in 2026 and taking slots for 2031 delivery. Smaller units can arrive sooner, but get a dated quote or a reservation agreement before relying on any schedule.

faqs.question: Do on-site gas turbines need an air permit?
faqs.answer: Yes. The permit class depends on potential emissions. Under EPA's Title V rules, 100 tons per year of any pollutant, or 10 tons per year of a single hazardous air pollutant, makes a major source, with lower thresholds in some nonattainment areas. The xAI disputes in Memphis and Southaven show the cost of running turbines before the permit record is settled.

faqs.question: Can a Texas data center take power directly from an existing power plant?
faqs.answer: Possibly, but SB 6 requires ERCOT study and PUCT approval for net metering arrangements between new large loads and existing generators, unless an exemption applies. The PUCT adopted the implementing rule on March 26, 2026. Check whether the arrangement has been filed and what conditions were set.

faqs.question: Is on-site gas power cheaper than grid power?
faqs.answer: Not always. Lazard's 2026 figures put gas combined cycle at $51 to $129 per MWh and gas peaking at $144 to $276 per MWh, and small on-site units usually sit closer to peaker economics. Cheap local gas, such as Permian supply during pipeline constraints, can change the math, though that discount may narrow as new pipelines open.

faqs.question: How does Invariant evaluate a behind-the-meter site?
faqs.answer: Invariant applies the same power evidence ladder it uses for grid sites, with gas supply, air permits and equipment as the rungs. A pipeline on a map counts as proximity. A written capacity figure, a permit covering the full build-out and an equipment reservation move a site up a tier.

title: Data center acres per MW: land sizing for AI campuses, colocation and mining
description: How many acres a data center needs per MW: PUE, rack density, substation and cooling footprints, real campus examples and a quick check of listing acreage against MW.
intro: A modern data center campus needs roughly 0.5 to 2 acres of gross land per MW of total facility load, and a bitcoin mine can get by on a quarter of that. Those are rules of thumb, not standards. The building itself is a small share of the site. Substations, cooling yards, generators, stormwater ponds, setbacks and land held for later phases take most of it. This guide shows how to size the land from the power number, what each piece of infrastructure takes, how announced campuses compare, and how to check whether a listing's acreage fits the MW it claims.
takeaways: Size land from total facility load (IT load times PUE), not from rack count or building area.
Buildings cover a small share of an AI campus. Fairwater puts about 1.2 million square feet of floor area on 315 acres.
Reserve about 3 acres for a 138 kV substation and 8.5 to 16.5 acres for 345 kV before laying out halls, using ComEd's 2026 guidelines as a reference.
Acreage almost never limits a site. Check usable acres for fit, then ask for the utility document behind the MW.

sections.heading: Size the load before you size the land

blocks.text: Every acreage question starts with a power number, and there are two of them. IT load is what the servers draw. Total facility load adds cooling, power conversion losses, lighting and offices. The ratio between them is power usage effectiveness, or PUE. Uptime Institute put the average per-site PUE across its survey at 1.58 for 2023, and 1.47 when weighted by IT capacity, with large new hyperscale builds designed for 1.4 or lower and some cloud operators claiming 1.2 or lower at certain sites.

So a 100 MW IT campus at a PUE of 1.3 needs about 130 MW at the meter. The utility sizes its service to the facility number. The land plan has to hold the gear for both: the halls for the IT load and the yards for everything that turns 130 MW into 100 MW of useful compute. Ask which number a listing means when it says "100 MW." Brokers often don't say.

Rack density is the other input, and it has split the market in two. Uptime's 2025 survey found average densities still rising slowly, driven by racks in the 10 to 30 kW range, with few facilities above 30 kW.
AI racks sit far above that. NVIDIA's GB200 NVL72 rack is rated at about 120 kW and is direct liquid cooled, roughly double the rack designs that came before it.

Higher density shrinks the white space per MW. It doesn't shrink the substation, the chillers or the dry coolers, because those scale with heat and power, not with how tightly servers are packed. That's why a dense AI campus can still need a lot of land. The building gets smaller per MW while the yard around it stays about the same size per MW.

sections.heading: Most of a campus is not building

blocks.text: Microsoft's Fairwater AI campus in Mount Pleasant, Wisconsin is a useful reference. Microsoft describes three buildings with about 1.2 million square feet under roof on a 315-acre site. That is about 28 acres of floor area. Even if every square foot sat on one level, the roofs would cover less than a tenth of the land. The same post describes a water-cooled chiller plant, a closed-loop system and 172 twenty-foot fans on cooling fins along the buildings.
A concept plan should show all of the following before anyone quotes MW per acre.

items: On-site substation. ComEd's January 2026 guidelines call for at least 784 by 472 feet (about 8.5 acres) for a 345 kV interconnection substation on one line, expandable to 784 by 914 feet (about 16.5 acres), and 413 by 324 feet (about 3.1 acres) for 138 kV, all excluding stormwater detention.
Customer substation. PSE&G's data center guidance lists 2.5 acres of equipment space at 69, 138 and 230 kV, 2.5 to 5 acres at 345 kV and 7 acres at 500 kV.

Generator yards and fuel. Diesel or gas backup units, belly tanks or bulk fuel storage, and the separation and noise screening around them. Many campuses line the generators along the long walls of each hall.
Heat rejection. Air-cooled chillers, dry coolers, or cooling towers, on the roof or in a ground-level yard. Liquid-cooled AI halls still reject heat outside.
Water. Storage tanks for fire protection and, for evaporative designs, makeup water and treatment.
Stormwater detention. Ponds or vaults sized to local rules, which grow with every acre of roof and pavement.
Setbacks, buffers and screening. Zoning setbacks from property lines and residential uses, plus berms and landscaping that noise and visual conditions often require.
Roads, parking, security and laydown. Perimeter fencing, guard posts, truck access and construction staging.
Future phases. Pad sites held for the second and third buildings, and a second substation position.

blocks.text: The substation figures come from two utilities and are not a national standard. Still, they set a floor. A 345 kV switching station plus a customer substation can take 10 to 20 acres before a single hall goes up.

Behind-the-meter generation adds its own footprint: turbines or reciprocating engines, gas metering and regulation, switchyard, emissions controls and the setback from the property line that an air permit and a noise study usually require. Crusoe's 1.2 GW Abilene campus pairs a grid interconnection with behind-the-meter batteries and solar, and gas turbines for backup power. Solar needs far more acreage per MW than the data center it supports.

sections.heading: MW per acre by facility type

blocks.text: The ranges below are Invariant's working rules of thumb for gross acres, measured against total facility load at full build. They are not published standards. Real projects land outside them for good reasons, usually stories, cooling type or land held for later phases.

rows: Bitcoin mining (containers or air-cooled sheds)
2 to 5
Single-story, little redundancy, no generator yard, minimal parking. Density limited mainly by airflow, noise setbacks and the substation.
Enterprise or colocation, suburban
Lower rack density, generator yard sized for full redundancy, more parking and office space, often one or two stories.
Enterprise or colocation, urban multi-story
2 to 6
Three or more stories, rooftop heat rejection, tight lot lines. The land is expensive, so the building goes up.
Hyperscale cloud campus
Many halls, large generator and chiller yards, buffers to neighbors and land held for future phases.
AI training campus (liquid cooled, 100+ kW racks)
Dense halls but large heat rejection yards, high-voltage substations and phased pads for multi-GW plans.
Campus with on-site gas generation
Adds the plant, gas yard, switchyard and air-permit setbacks. Solar or batteries on site push the ratio lower still.

blocks.text: Public campus numbers sit inside those bands. The examples below divide announced MW by announced acres. Treat them as rough: acreage and MW are reported at different dates, and "capacity" in a press release can mean IT load, facility load or a compute figure.

rows: Riot Platforms, Corsicana, Texas (bitcoin mining)
1,000 planned, 400 MW first phase
About 3.8 at full build
Crusoe, Abilene, Texas (AI campus)
1,100 for the wider Abilene Clean Campus
About 1.1, counting the whole campus
Meta Hyperion, Richland Parish, Louisiana (AI)
2,000 original plan, 5,000 expanded
2,250 original, about 1,400 added
About 0.9 original, about 1.4 expanded
Microsoft Fairwater, Mount Pleasant, Wisconsin (AI)
Not published
Not computable

blocks.text: Riot's 265 acres were bought for a 1 GW mining site energized from a 400 MW substation in its first phase. Crusoe's eight buildings total about 4 million square feet, which is roughly 92 acres of floor area for 1.2 GW. Meta's original Hyperion plan was nine buildings with about 4 million square feet on 2,250 acres, and the campus was expanded to 5 GW in July 2026 after Meta added roughly 1,400 adjacent acres.

sections.heading: Land is rarely the binding constraint

blocks.text: Run the numbers on almost any rural listing and the land is ample. A 300-acre parcel at 1 MW per acre holds 300 MW. The question is whether 300 MW can be delivered there, and by when.

Paces ran a power-flow analysis on ERCOT's 2028 summer-peak planning case and found that only about 17% of substations near land suitable for data centers had positive withdrawal headroom. In other words, most substations with good parcels next to them could not take new load without making existing overloads worse.

That result matches what we see. Search from power evidence first and then find the parcel, not the other way round. We grade power claims on a ladder. Rung 0 is a map. Rung 1 is proximity to a line or substation of the right voltage. Rung 2 is a named MW figure at a named station from a utility or planning record, or an existing large connection such as a retired plant's export capacity or an energized load. Rung 3 is a utility study or approval for this load. Rung 4 is an executed service or interconnection agreement with a date, or service that is already energized and metered.
A broker's "450 MW available" sits at rung 2 until a current utility letter is in hand. Acreage doesn't move a site up the ladder at all.

sections.heading: Usable acres are smaller than gross acres

blocks.text: Listings quote gross acres. A campus gets built on usable acres, and the gap between the two can be a third of the parcel or more. Take these off before dividing MW by acres:

items: Wetlands and streams, which usually need a delineation and may need a federal permit to fill.
Mapped floodplain, where critical electrical and mechanical equipment belongs above the base flood elevation, if it goes there at all.
Steep slope, which adds grading cost and limits the large flat pads that halls and substations need.
Easements: existing transmission, pipeline, rail and road rights of way that cross the parcel and cannot be built on.
Zoning setbacks and any buffer conditions from a rezoning or special use permit.
Irregular shape. A long thin parcel can lose much of its area to setbacks on both sides.

blocks.text: Utility siting rules bite here too. ComEd wants the interconnection substation reachable from at least two sides for future lines, with no river, forest, wetland or other transmission line on those sides, and within half a mile of the existing line. The developer also buys the land for the tie-line, the access road and the substation's own stormwater detention. A parcel that looks big on a map can fail those tests at the one corner near the line.

sections.heading: Sites from our inventory that show the point

blocks.text: Listings in our inventory show why acreage alone says little about capacity.

rows: Arizona
Listing claims 1,000 MW with no utility document cited.
About 100,000 acres
Candidate. Land is not the constraint here; the power claim is.
Houston, Texas
50 MW studied and approved per the listing, available mid-2027, 138 kV line under a mile away.
About 25 acres
Candidate. About 2 MW per acre, dense but workable for a single-building campus.
Western Kentucky
Former 443 MW plant, switchyard on site.
About 500 acres
Kept. Under 1 MW per acre leaves room for phases, buffers and on-site generation.

blocks.text: Divide the claimed MW by the usable acres before anything else. A ratio far outside the ranges above usually means the MW figure or the acreage needs a second look. Locations, owners and documents are shared on a call.

sections.heading: How to sanity-check a listing's acreage against its MW

blocks.text: This takes about ten minutes with a parcel map and the listing sheet.

items: Pin down which MW is quoted: IT load, facility load, or a utility service figure. Convert with a PUE of 1.2 to 1.5 if needed.
Find the usable acres. Subtract wetlands, floodplain, slope and easements from the gross figure.
Reserve the substation. Use about 3 acres at 138 kV and 8.5 to 16.5 acres at 345 kV as a starting reference, plus detention.
Divide facility MW by usable acres and compare with the table above for the facility type the buyer plans to build.

If the ratio is far above the band, the listing is overstating MW or assuming stories and rooftop cooling it hasn't designed. If it is far below, ask whether the extra land is for on-site generation, future phases or simply for sale at a higher price.
Then ignore the ratio and ask for the power document. Where does the MW figure sit on the evidence ladder?

blocks.text: Before parcel work goes far, clear the disqualifiers. Is the site already claimed, under option or operating? Is it listed with another buyer in diligence, or owned by an environmental-liability buyer? Is there coal ash or contamination, or a county moratorium? Any one of those ends the review regardless of acreage.

Invariant screens sites this way before any introduction. We sort them into three tiers: A for documented power, B for a named power path with a date, and C for land near capacity without either. Acreage is a check on the claim. The power document is the claim.

faqs.question: How many acres does a 100 MW data center need?
faqs.answer: As a rule of thumb, a 100 MW hyperscale or AI campus needs roughly 50 to 150 gross acres, including substation, cooling yards, generators, stormwater and buffers. A bitcoin mine of the same size can fit on 20 to 50 acres. A multi-story urban colocation building can use far less. These are working ranges, not standards, and usable acres matter more than gross acres.

faqs.question: How many MW per acre is typical for a data center?
faqs.answer: Most US campuses land between about 0.5 and 2 MW per gross acre of total facility load. Announced examples include Meta's original Hyperion plan at about 0.9 MW per acre and Riot's Corsicana mining site at about 3.8 MW per acre at full build. Stories, cooling type and land held for future phases explain most of the spread.

faqs.question: How much land does a data center substation take?
faqs.answer: ComEd's January 2026 guidelines call for at least 784 by 472 feet, about 8.5 acres, for a 345 kV interconnection substation on one line, expandable to about 16.5 acres, and about 3.1 acres at 138 kV, excluding stormwater detention. PSE&G lists 2.5 acres of equipment space at 69 to 230 kV and 7 acres at 500 kV. Check the serving utility's own standard.

faqs.question: Do AI racks reduce the land a data center needs?
faqs.answer: They reduce white space per MW, since a GB200 NVL72 rack draws about 120 kW versus 10 to 30 kW for typical racks. They do not reduce the substation, heat rejection or backup power, which scale with MW. Land per MW falls less than the rack numbers suggest.

faqs.question: How does Invariant check whether a site's acreage fits its MW?
faqs.answer: Invariant works out usable acres, reserves room for the substation and detention, and compares facility MW per usable acre with the range for the planned facility type. Then it looks for the utility document behind the MW figure. A site only moves up a tier on power evidence, not on acreage.

title: Data center moratoriums: how to screen a county before you option land
description: How to check a US county for data center moratoriums, rezoning fights and new ordinances before optioning land, with 2025 to 2026 cases and a practical kill sheet.
intro: Screen the county before you screen the parcel. In 2025 and 2026, data center projects with land under contract were stopped by moratoriums, court rulings on rezonings, withdrawn petitions, and outright municipal bans. Most of those signals were public before anyone signed an option: a pending ordinance on a planning commission agenda, a packed hearing on a nearby project, a county with no zoning power and a lawsuit already filed. Run a short local-approval check alongside the power check, and write what you find into the option terms.
takeaways: Check for an active or proposed moratorium in both the county and any city that could annex the site. They are separate governments with separate clocks.
Find out whether a data center is a by-right use, a conditional or special use, or needs a rezoning. A vote is a risk you can price; an unknown path is not.
Treat recent denials, withdrawals and lawsuits within the same county as the best predictor of how the next hearing goes.
Size option periods and extension rights to the local calendar: moratorium expiry dates, hearing schedules and elections.

sections.heading: Local approval is now a gate, not a formality

blocks.text: Data Center Watch, a tracker of community opposition, counted at least 75 US data center projects worth about $130 billion as blocked or delayed in the first quarter of 2026 alone. It also reported more than 300 state data center bills filed in the first six weeks of the year, and statewide moratorium proposals in 14 states. Its definition of delayed is broad and includes extended reviews and lawsuits, so read the totals as a measure of friction, not of cancelled megawatts.

The friction lands on land. A buyer can hold a utility study for 300 MW and still lose the site because the county board pauses applications for six months, or because a judge voids the rezoning on a notice defect two years later. Power is still the scarce input. But a parcel with documented power and no workable path to a building permit is a stranded option.

The fix is cheap. Most of the evidence sits in agendas, minutes, local news and court dockets. It takes a few hours per county, and it belongs in the kill sheet before any title, survey or environmental spend.

sections.heading: What the 2025 to 2026 cases show

blocks.text: The table below lists cases that each show a different way a site dies or stalls. Status is as of November 2026.

rows: Prince William County, Virginia (Digital Gateway, about 2,100 acres)
A circuit court voided the rezonings in August 2025 over public notice failures. The Court of Appeals affirmed on March 31, 2026.
The county and one developer dropped appeals in April 2026. The last developer withdrew its Supreme Court appeal on July 2, 2026. The rezonings stay void.
Tucson and Pima County, Arizona (Project Blue, 290 acres)
Pima County approved the land sale and project. Tucson's council voted unanimously on August 6, 2025 to stop city work on it, after opposition over water and energy.
Pima County planners voted 8 to 1 on October 28, 2026 to advance stricter data center rules, with a Board of Supervisors hearing expected in early December 2026.
City of St. Charles, Missouri
One-year moratorium on applications in August 2025.
Converted to a ban on large-scale data center development in May 2026.
St. Charles County, Missouri
Six-month moratorium approved unanimously in July 2026 on developments over 100,000 square feet or 5 MW.
Active. A motion to extend it to 12 months failed amid doubt over whether state law allows more than six months at a time.
Georgia counties and cities
Coweta, Clayton, Troup, Pike, Lamar and LaGrange among those adopting moratoriums in 2025. Others wrote ordinances with noise limits, buffers and cooling water rules.
Most were short pauses. Coweta's 180-day pause was set to expire in November 2025 with a draft ordinance pending. Check each county's current code rather than the 2025 headlines.
Indianapolis (Franklin Township), Indiana
A 468-acre rezoning petition was withdrawn on September 22, 2025, before a City-County Council vote, after organized opposition over water and electric bills.
Withdrawn, not denied, so it could return. No refiling reported in the source.
Hood and Hill Counties, Texas
Hood County commissioners rejected moratorium votes twice in February 2026, then revoked a concept plan and were sued. Hill County adopted a one-year pause in May 2026.
Hill County faces a developer lawsuit seeking $100 million. County authority to pause development in unincorporated areas is contested.

blocks.text: Three patterns repeat. First, the approval itself can be undone: Prince William's rezonings passed and were later voided on procedure, so a granted rezoning with litigation pending is not an entitled site. Second, a city and its county can act in opposite directions on the same land, as Tucson and Pima County did. Third, a moratorium is often a step toward a permanent rule. St. Charles went from a one-year pause to a ban in nine months.

sections.heading: State actions change the cost of a site, not just its approval

blocks.text: States have mostly acted through utility rates and tax law rather than siting bans. These changes shift who pays for grid upgrades and how long a buyer is locked in, which changes the value of an option.

items: Georgia: in January 2025 the Public Service Commission approved a Georgia Power rule letting it bill new customers above 100 MW on special terms, including upstream generation and transmission costs, minimum bills and contracts of up to 15 years instead of 5. Every such contract goes to the PSC for review.

Texas: SB 6, signed in June 2025, applies to loads of 75 MW or more in ERCOT. It requires disclosure of duplicate interconnection requests elsewhere in Texas, sets a $100,000 minimum initial interconnection fee, and requires large loads to accept curtailment during firm load shed with shutoff equipment installed.

Minnesota: the 2025 data center law adds an annual fee of $2 million to $5 million for large data centers based on peak demand, ends the sales tax exemption on their electricity, orders a very large customer class at the PUC, and sets special permit conditions for consumptive water use above 100 million gallons a year.

blocks.text: These are state-level facts a seller's broker rarely mentions. They also feed local politics. In November 2025 Georgia voters replaced two incumbent PSC commissioners with challengers who won close to 63% of the vote, in races that centered on power bills. Local officials read those results.

sections.heading: What triggers opposition

blocks.text: The concerns are concrete and they show up in ordinance text. When a county writes a data center ordinance, it usually turns each complaint into a standard. Read the standard and you know what the last fight was about.

items: Water. Forsyth County, Georgia bars data center cooling systems from the county water system, and Jones County requires closed-loop cooling. Water was the main complaint in Tucson and Indianapolis.
Noise. Bartow County, Georgia caps data center noise at 65 dB by day and 55 dB at night, with a 200-foot property buffer.
Power bills. Ratepayer impact is now a standard objection, and it drove the Georgia PSC races.
Backup generators. Large diesel fleets bring air permits, fuel storage and testing noise, and neighbors raise them at hearings.
Secrecy. Pima County commissioners said Project Blue came to them under a non-disclosure agreement and that they were misled. Code names and NDAs now draw suspicion on their own.
Tax breaks. Abatements and sales tax exemptions are a common complaint where a project asks for them, and Minnesota has already narrowed one.

blocks.text: A site that needs a water main extension, sits within earshot of a subdivision and relies on a county tax abatement carries every one of these at once. A site on an existing industrial park with closed-loop cooling and no incentive request carries far fewer.

sections.heading: The county kill sheet

blocks.text: Run this before any parcel work, next to the power check. A red on the first row usually ends the site. The rest set the price, the option length and the contingencies.

rows: Active moratorium in the county or a city that could annex the site
Board and council agendas and minutes for the last 12 months; local news; county code updates
Stop unless the expiry date and the replacement ordinance are both known. Check whether the pause covers applications, approvals or permits.
Proposed moratorium or data center ordinance in draft
Planning commission agendas, staff reports, public hearing notices
Expect new standards on noise, water, setbacks or size. Model the site against the draft, not the current code.
Zoning path
Use table, definitions and conditional use standards in the zoning ordinance
By-right use in the current district is the strongest position. Special or conditional use means a public hearing. A rezoning means a legislative vote and a litigation window.
Recent denials, withdrawals or court challenges in the county
Minutes, local news, state court dockets
Opposition is already organized. A withdrawn petition can return, and so can the people who opposed it.
County land-use authority
State enabling law; county attorney opinions; whether the county has adopted zoning at all
An unzoned county or one with limited powers, as in unincorporated Texas, may mean fewer approvals but more lawsuits and less predictability.
Upcoming elections and hearing dates
County election calendar; board meeting schedule; PSC election calendar
A board that changes in January can reverse course. Time filings to avoid hearings in the weeks before an election.
Local utility stance
Utility economic development pages, large-load tariffs, recent rate cases
A utility filing for a new large-load class or collateral rule signals what service will cost and how local officials will be briefed.
Community benefit expectations
Recent development agreements and host fees in the county or nearby
Sets the cost of approval. A county that negotiated a host agreement last year will expect one again.
Water source and provider position
Municipal water policy, large water user ordinances, state permit thresholds
Bans on potable water for cooling or volume thresholds can force a closed-loop design or end the site.

blocks.text: Score each row green, amber or red, and write down the document behind each color. A blank cell is not green. In Invariant's power evidence terms, a site with a rung 3 utility study in a county with a live moratorium is still a C until the local path is known.

sections.heading: Structure land options around the local risk

blocks.text: The kill sheet will not clear every risk. Some sites are worth optioning with an open local question. Write the question into the contract so it costs the buyer time, not the deposit.

items: Make the option period match the real calendar. If a six-month moratorium is in force, add its remaining term, the hearing cycle for the replacement ordinance and the approval process itself. St. Charles County debated whether Missouri law allows a pause longer than six months at a time, which makes back-to-back renewals the likely tool. Plan for at least one.
Tie extensions to public events. Give the buyer paid extensions that trigger automatically if a moratorium is extended or a zoning hearing is continued.

Add an entitlement contingency with a clear definition. A rezoning or special use approval should count only when final and unappealable, or once the appeal period has run with no suit filed. The Prince William rezonings were approved and then voided in court.
Include an annexation clause for sites near a city boundary. If the land could be annexed, the buyer needs the right to exit if the city's rules apply and they forbid the use.
Cap the deposit at risk during the entitlement phase, and release it only after approvals are final.
Keep the seller cooperative. Require signatures on applications and attendance at hearings where useful, and stop the seller from marketing the site while the option runs.
Avoid an NDA that keeps the county in the dark. Some confidentiality is normal. A board that learns the end user's identity late may react the way Pima County's commissioners did.

blocks.text: Invariant runs this county screen before any site introduction. A moratorium, a voided rezoning or a contested county power question goes on the kill sheet with the source, and the site is tiered on power and local path together.

faqs.question: What is a data center moratorium?
faqs.answer: It is a temporary local pause on accepting or approving data center applications while the government studies the use and writes rules. St. Charles County, Missouri adopted a six-month moratorium in July 2026 on developments over 100,000 square feet or 5 MW. Some moratoriums end in a new ordinance and some end in a ban.

faqs.question: Can a Texas county stop a data center in an unincorporated area?
faqs.answer: Its powers are limited. Texas counties generally lack the zoning authority that cities have. Hood County commissioners twice voted down a moratorium in February 2026 over legal concerns, and Hill County was sued after it adopted a one-year pause in May 2026.

faqs.question: Is a rezoning approval final once the board votes?
faqs.answer: Not until any challenge is resolved. Prince William County's Digital Gateway rezonings were approved, then voided in court over public notice defects, and the ruling held through the last appeal in July 2026. Treat a rezoning as secure only once the challenge window closes.

faqs.question: Which states have changed rules for large data center loads?
faqs.answer: Georgia, Texas and Minnesota are three examples. Georgia lets Georgia Power apply special terms and longer contracts to new loads above 100 MW. Texas SB 6 sets rules for loads of 75 MW or more in ERCOT, and Minnesota added an annual fee and a very large customer class.

faqs.question: How does Invariant check local risk on a site?
faqs.answer: Invariant runs a county kill sheet before any introduction: moratoriums, the zoning path, recent denials and lawsuits, county authority and the utility's position. A site with good power but an open local question is tiered lower until the question is answered.
